Other second-line drugs are phenytoin, clobazam, or the newer antiepileptics gabapentin, levetiracetam, tiagabine, or zonisa- mide,16,23,29 but whether these are recommended for mono- therapy or adjunctive treatment may vary from country to country. Other drugs that have been used16 include aceta- zolamide, clonazepam, and the barbiturates phenobarbital or primidone, although the latter in particular are little used now because of the problems of sedation. Vigabatrin is li- censed in the UK for adjunctive use in patients in whom all other combinations have failed. The response rate is somewhat lower for partial seizures than for tonic-clonic seizures associated with primary gen- eralised epilepsy (see below). There is some evidence in favour of carbamazepine rather than valproate in the treat- ment of partial seizures.30 More recently, some evidence was found in favour of lamotrigine rather than car- bamazepine,31,32 and of oxcarbazepine rather than pheny- toin,33 in terms of tolerability and time to treatment failure. However, there is no evidence of any significant difference between phenytoin and carbamazepine34 or valproate35 in partial seizures. Calcium-channel blockers such as flunarizine have been studied with equivocal results in patients with refractory epilepsy, particularly those with partial seizures.36 The drugs used most often to treat generalised tonic-clon- ic seizures are carbamazepine, lamotrigine, or valproate. For tonic-clonic seizures as part of the syndrome of prima- ry generalised epilepsy, valproate is the drug of choice, al- though systematic reviews were unable to establish evi- dence for this.30,35 Topiramate is also considered a first choice in patients in whom the other older drugs are unsuitable or ineffective.16,22 More recently, valproate was found to be better tolerated than topiramate and more ef- fective than lamotrigine in generalised and unclassified epilepsy.37 Second-line drugs in UK guidelines are cloba- zam, levetiracetam, and oxcarbazepine,
